newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Papal envoy says Burundi killers face God.
newsitem.headline: Papal envoy says Burundi killers face God.

text.p: Thousands of Catholics paid their last respects on Tuesday to Burundi's murdered archbishop with the church saying killers stalking the violent country might escape on earth but they faced God's justice.
"Woe to those who think to seat their throne on the tombs on the men, women and children of this country," Cardinal Jozef Tomko, Pope John Paul's special envoy, told a memorial service.
"The conscience of the world always demands justice for the innocent. And if the wrongdoers escape the justice of men, they will not be able to escape the justice of God," he warned.
He lashed out against ethnic killing in the central town of Gitega where thousands of Roman Catholics honoured Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna, Burundi's senior prelate killed in an ambush last week.

Four people survived the attack north of Gitega town blamed by the army and priests on ethnic Hutu rebels. The bodies of the 62-year-old archbishop and a nun killed with him were not found. But the corpse of another nun was recovered by rescuers.
Hutu rebels blamed the Tutsi-dominated army for the attack.
Bishops joined dozens of priests and nuns for the service in Gitega, the second largest city in a country being torn apart by massacres and war between the rebels and the army.
Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya, who seized power from the civilian Hutu president in a coup on July 25, attended the service and took communion from Tomko in the cathedral.
Tomko said ethnic conflict had transformed Burundi from the "Switzerland of Africa" into a land of massacre and destruction.
"To you political leaders, members of different parties, soldiers, armed groups, in the name of God stop the massacre of Burundians, stop the killing," he said.

More than 150,000 people have been killed in three years of civil war in Burundi, which many fear may go the way of neighbouring Rwanda where up to an estimated one million people were killed in genocide in 1994.
Troops with automatic weapons watched some 2,000 people crowded onto benches in the stone cathedral while about the same number stood outside listening to the sermon.
Soldiers in black and green berets poked back the faithful pushing to get into the cathdral as Burundian priests in white and red cassocks offered up prayers in French and Kirundi.
The congregation, which included Hutus and Tutsis, sang along with the choir, accompanied by an electronic organ.
Soldiers lined streets in Gitega town and appeared every few hundred metres (yards) on the road between Gitega and Bujumbura, the Burundian capital 105 km (65 miles) to the northwest.
Tomko urged Burundians to follow the archbishop's example by working for peace though his family were destroyed in fighting.
"Do not allow yourselves to be manipulated by those preaching the message of death and hate," the cardinal said.
Tomko said the Pope was saddened by the death of Ruhuna, whose killing he called a grave wound not only to the Church but also to Burundi, a Roman Catholic country he visited in 1990.
Landlocked Burundi has been hobbled by economic sanctions imposed by its neighbours since July 31 in an effort to punish Buyoya's government for the coup and force him to talk to the rebels.
